cards.q: What is data flow in networking?
cards.a: Data flow is the lifecycle of a unit of data from a source application to a destination application across a network: encapsulation down the source, transmission across intermediate devices, and decapsulation up the destination, plus the peer-to-peer and directional concepts that frame each journey.

cards.q: Describe the 7-step end-to-end journey of data.
cards.a: 1) App generates data; 2) Down the stack: transport adds ports (segment), network adds IP (packet), link adds Ethernet (frame), physical sends bits; 3) Each switch forwards by destination MAC and re-encapsulates a new L2 header; 4) Each router strips Ethernet, checks TTL/sum, looks up the route, and rewrites a new L2 header; 5) NAT/tunnel/firewall devices may alter addresses mid-path; 6) Destination decapsulates up to the app; 7) The application replies in reverse (full duplex possible).

cards.q: What does the 'peer-to-peer' concept mean in the OSI model?
cards.a: Peer layers talk to their peers logically: TCP at A understands TCP at B, and OSPF at each router talks to OSPF on its neighbor, even though machines exchange frames on the wire. It is the logical same-layer-to-same-layer relationship, not file sharing.

cards.q: What are the four directional classes of data flow and their examples?
cards.a: Unicast (one source to one destination: normal HTTP, SSH), Broadcast (one to all on the segment: ARP request, DHCP discover), Multicast (one group to subscribed members: video feed, OSPF hello), and Anycast (one address to the nearest of several: DNS anycast, VRRP anycast gateway).

cards.q: What is the difference between anycast and multicast?
cards.a: Anycast sends to the nearest of several identical destinations sharing one address (e.g. DNS anycast), while multicast sends to a group of subscribed members. Where each device receives the traffic is the key distinction, frequently tested at L3/IPv6.

cards.q: What is a flow's identity in TCP/IP?
cards.a: A TCP flow is identified by the 5-tuple: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, and protocol. This is used by NetFlow, ACLs, and firewalls to identify a flow, and real-time UDP RTP flows use the same concept for QoS classification.

cards.q: How do switches, routers, ACLs/firewalls, and load balancers control data flow?
cards.a: Switches filter/forward based on the MAC table; routers pick the next hop by longest-prefix match; ACLs/firewalls accept or drop by the 5-tuple; QoS marks and queues flows; load balancers distribute flows across servers.

cards.q: What changes to destination MAC and to source/destination IP as data hops across a network?
cards.a: The destination MAC (and source MAC) change on every link, but the source and destination IPs typically remain constant unless NAT is applied.

cards.q: Should you say 'the frame travels over the router'?
cards.a: No. Routers strip the L2 header, so a full IP packet is routed and the L2 frame is recreated on each link. The frame itself does not travel across the router.

cards.q: What happens to TTL as a packet is routed?
cards.a: TTL always decreases with each router (L3) forwarding hop.

cards.q: What command shows the next-hop CEF path for a flow, and what captures flow records?
cards.a: show ip fib shows the CEF next-hop for a flow. NetFlow captures flow records with commands such as ip flow-export destination, plus traceroute and ping observe the flow journey.
